When you order food, you do not need to stand frozen at the counter. An asynchronous method can wait for I/O and let the thread do other useful work.

How to test this example in Visual Studio

Download the project below, extract it into its own folder, then open StudyLab.csproj. Wait for NuGet restore. Choose Build → Build Solution. For console projects choose Start Without Debugging. For API projects use View → Terminal, make sure the terminal is in the folder containing StudyLab.csproj, then run the command shown in the lesson. Do not paste all files into Program.cs: use the exact file names displayed below.

Follow a Task

static async Task<string> LoadAsync(string name)
{
    await Task.Delay(20);
    return name;
}
var values = await Task.WhenAll(LoadAsync("A"), LoadAsync("B"));
Console.WriteLine(string.Join(",", values));

Expected: A,B. The operations overlap their waiting time. WhenAll returns results in input order, not completion order. Use async Task for work and async Task<T> for a result. async void is mainly for event handlers.

Cancellation and errors

Pass a CancellationToken into HTTP, database and delay methods. A cancelled task usually throws OperationCanceledException at await. A task failure is rethrown at await; handle it where you can recover. Avoid .Result or .Wait on a UI thread. Do not hold a lock across await. For CPU work use a bounded amount of parallel work, rather than launching unlimited tasks.

Try it yourself

Why use Task.Delay instead of Thread.Sleep in an async demo?

Worked answer

Task.Delay yields while waiting. Thread.Sleep blocks the current thread.

Rewrite two sequential downloads as overlapping I/O.

Worked answer

Create both tasks first, then await Task.WhenAll. Still limit concurrency for large batches.
